intro.text: The New Testament uses the name Herod for three men: the king of Matthew 2 and Luke 1, the tetrarch of the Gospels and Acts 13:1, and the king of Acts 12. It names three more rulers of the family: Archelaus, Philip the tetrarch and King Agrippa.
Scripture states only three family links among them: Archelaus reigned "in the room of his father Herod"; Philip was the tetrarch's brother; and Herodias had been "his brother Philip's wife".

Dates are reconstructions. These pages give Schürer's (1890): Herod the Great king 37–4 BC; Archelaus 4 BC – AD 6; Antipas 4 BC – AD 39; Philip 4 BC – AD 34; Agrippa I AD 37–44; Agrippa II about AD 50–100. Other views are shown on each page.

Scripture gives none of these men a regnal verdict. Each page shows what the text says of him, quoted as it stands; for four of them, that means their dealings with Jesus, John the Baptist, the apostles or Paul.

rulers.name: Herod the Great
rulers.title: King of Judaea, under Rome
rulers.tagline: King in Jerusalem when Jesus was born in Bethlehem.

capital.name: Jerusalem
capital.note: Matthew finds him in Jerusalem, where "all Jerusalem" was troubled with him.

identifications.text: Matthew calls him only "Herod the king" and Luke "Herod, the king of Judaea". Matthew ties him to the rest of the family in one phrase: Archelaus reigned "in the room of his father Herod".

"Herod's judgment hall" at Caesarea, where Paul was kept, is taken by commentators to be the palace Herod the Great had built there and the governors later used (Poole, 1683; Meyer, English translation 1877–1879; Vincent, 1887). Acts does not say which Herod built it.

reign.text: Not given in Scripture: Jesus was born "in the days of Herod the king", and the family stayed in Egypt "until the death of Herod".

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: None. Matthew and Luke date events by his reign (Matthew 2:1; Luke 1:5) but give no years.

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: Made king by the Roman Senate late in 40 BC; took Jerusalem in 37 BC; died at Jericho shortly before the Passover of 4 BC.

dates.label: A later death: 3 BC or 1 BC (minority, as listed by Schürer)
dates.note: Quandt and Kellner put his death in 3 BC; Caspari and Riess in 1 BC (Schürer, 1890, p. 466, lists them without their reasons).

scriptureSays.text: Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea "in the days of Herod the king", when wise men came from the east to Jerusalem asking, "Where is he that is born King of the Jews?"

"When Herod the king had heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him." He asked the chief priests and scribes where Christ should be born, and they answered, "In Bethlehem of Judaea."
He called the wise men privately, "enquired of them diligently what time the star appeared", and sent them to Bethlehem: "bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also."
Warned of God in a dream, the wise men did not return to Herod. An angel told Joseph, "Herod will seek the young child to destroy him", and the family fled into Egypt "until the death of Herod".

When he saw that he was mocked, he "was exceeding wroth" and "slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under", reckoning by the time the wise men had given him.
"But when Herod was dead", Matthew says, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt: "they are dead which sought the young child's life."
Luke dates the angel's announcement to Zacharias "in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea".
Scripture gives Herod no regnal record: no length of reign, no verdict formula, no burial. Everything it says of him belongs to the accounts of the births of John the Baptist and Jesus.

claim.text: Wise men from the east came to Jerusalem; Herod sent them to Bethlehem.
He slew the children of Bethlehem and its coasts, from two years old and under.

worship.text: Herod gathered "all the chief priests and scribes of the people" to ask where Christ should be born.
The temple of Jesus' day had been "Forty and six years" in building, the Jews said to Jesus at Jerusalem. John does not name the builder.

Schürer (1890) dates the start of Herod's rebuilding to the end of 20 or the beginning of 19 BC; counting the forty-six years from then, he places that Passover of John 2 in AD 27 or, "more probably", AD 28.

building.text: Schürer (1890) takes the Antiquities' eighteenth year, 20/19 BC, for the start of the temple work, and suggests the War's fifteenth year is wrong or counts the preparations.

people.text: "All Jerusalem" was troubled with him at the wise men's question.
Matthew sets Jeremiah's words of Rachel weeping in Rama beside the slaughter at Bethlehem.

person.name: Micah
person.note: Matthew says only "the prophet"; the words are those of Micah 5:2.

claim.text: The chief priests and scribes answered Herod's question from "the prophet": out of Bethlehem "shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel".

quote.text: And thou Bethlehem, in the land of Juda, art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come a Governor, that shall rule my people Israel.

claim.text: Matthew says the slaughter at Bethlehem fulfilled what was "spoken by Jeremy the prophet".

quote.text: In Rama was there a voice heard, lamentation, and weeping, and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.

outside.name: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.4.11
outside.date: written about four centuries after Herod

claim.text: A Latin writer, Macrobius, tells that Augustus, hearing that among the boys under two years old whom Herod king of the Jews ordered killed in Syria his own son had also been killed, said: "It is better to be Herod's pig than his son" (our translation of the Latin).

views.label: 3 BC
views.holders: Quandt and Kellner, as listed by Schürer (1890)

argument.text: Schürer names them as placing the death a year later; he does not set out their reasons.

views.label: 1 BC
views.holders: Caspari and Riess (1880), as listed by Schürer (1890)

argument.text: Schürer names them as diverging further, to 1 BC (and Seyffarth further still, to AD 1); he does not set out their reasons.

questions.question: Herod's death and the date of Jesus' birth

views.label: In Herod's last years; Luke's Quirinius is a mistake

argument.text: Schürer notes that Luke 1:5, as well as Matthew 2, assumes Jesus was born in Herod's lifetime. But Quirinius was not governor of Syria in Herod's last years, so Schürer holds that Luke's census (Luke 2:2) cannot belong to Herod's reign.

views.label: About 6 BC, at an enrolment held under Herod

argument.text: Ramsay argues that the first periodic enrolment of Syria was made in 8–7 BC, that Palestine's was delayed to the late summer or autumn of 6 BC, and that Quirinius then commanded Syria's armies; Jesus was born then.

questions.question: Why does no other ancient record tell of the children of Bethlehem?

views.label: Macrobius remembers it
views.holders: John Gill (1746–1748); F. W. Farrar (1874, quoted in the Pulpit Commentary); W. M. Ramsay (1898)

argument.text: They read Macrobius's story as a mixed or dim memory of the slaughter. Ramsay thinks Macrobius did not take it from a Christian writer, because a Christian would have said Palestine, not Syria.

notSaid: Scripture never calls him "the Great".
Scripture gives no length of reign, no verdict formula and no burial for Herod.
Matthew does not say how many children died at Bethlehem.
Scripture does not say how Herod died or where he was buried.
The Gospels do not say who rebuilt the temple of Jesus' day; John 2:20 gives only its forty-six years of building.
Matthew does not say how long after the birth the wise men came; Herod's "two years old and under" is reckoned from the time of the star.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where the wise men came and Herod questioned them

places.name: Egypt
places.note: Where the family fled until Herod's death

places.name: Ramah
places.note: Named in the words of Jeremiah that Matthew quotes

rulers.name: Archelaus
rulers.title: Ruler of Judaea under Rome
rulers.tagline: The son whose rule in Judaea turned Joseph aside to Galilee.

identifications.text: Matthew names him once, as son of Herod: "Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod".
Schürer (1890) assigns him the coins inscribed, in Greek, "of Herod the ethnarch", since no other Herodian bore that title, and notes that the Roman historian Dio Cassius calls him Herod.

reign.text: Not given in Scripture: Matthew says only that he "did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod".

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: Ethnarch from Herod's death in 4 BC until Augustus deposed him and banished him to Vienne in Gaul in AD 6.

scriptureSays.text: "When he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither": Joseph, warned in a dream, turned aside into Galilee.
Joseph settled the family in "a city called Nazareth".
This is the only verse that names Archelaus. Scripture records nothing he did or said.

claim.text: Afraid of Archelaus, Joseph took the child and his mother to Galilee and Nazareth.

questions.question: Is Archelaus behind Jesus' parable of the nobleman (Luke 19:12–27)?

views.label: Yes, the story echoes his journey to Rome
views.holders: H. A. W. Meyer (English 1880); F. W. Farrar (1880); C. J. Ellicott's commentary (about 1880); A. B. Bruce (1897), who says the idea has been "very generally accepted" since Clericus and Wolf

argument.text: A nobleman goes "into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom" and his citizens send after him, "We will not have this man to reign over us". They compare Archelaus's journey to Augustus and the embassy of fifty sent against him (Antiquities 17.11.1); Farrar notes that Herod and Archelaus had both gone from Jericho to Rome to receive a kingdom, and Jesus told the parable near Jericho (Luke 19:1, 11).

views.label: Jesus would not have pictured himself by Archelaus
views.holders: Schanz, as reported by A. B. Bruce (1897), who disagrees

argument.text: Bruce reports Schanz's objection that Jesus would not choose so bad a man to stand for himself, and answers that Jesus also used an unjust judge and an unjust steward in parables.

notSaid: Scripture names Archelaus once (Matthew 2:22) and records nothing he did.
Scripture does not call him king or ethnarch; it says he "did reign".
Scripture does not record his removal by Augustus.
Luke's parable of the nobleman (Luke 19:12) names no ruler.

rulers.name: Herod Antipas
rulers.title: Tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, under Rome
rulers.tagline: The tetrarch who beheaded John the Baptist and questioned Jesus.

identifications.text: The Gospels and Acts call him "Herod the tetrarch", and Luke "tetrarch of Galilee"; Luke names Philip as his brother. Scripture never uses the name Antipas.
Schürer (1890) notes that Antipas is the only man called Herod who bore the title of tetrarch (his brother Philip was also a tetrarch, but is never called Herod).
The Herod of Jesus' trial is the same man: Pilate sent Jesus to him on learning that he was a Galilean and "belonged unto Herod's jurisdiction". Acts 4:27 looks back on that day.

Three verses say only "Herod": Jesus' warning about "the leaven of Herod", Joanna "the wife of Chuza Herod's steward", and the Pharisees' "Herod will kill thee". They are taken as the tetrarch from their setting: Jesus' work in Galilee and on the road, after "Herod was dead" (Matthew 2:19) and before the "Herod the king" of Acts 12.

reign.text: Not given in Scripture: Luke places him as "tetrarch of Galilee" in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar.

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: Tetrarch from Herod's death in 4 BC until Gaius (Caligula) deposed him, in the summer of AD 39 by Schürer's reckoning; his coins run to the forty-third year of his rule.

scriptureSays.text: John the Baptist reproved "Herod the tetrarch" "for Herodias his brother Philip's wife, and for all the evils which Herod had done", and Herod "shut up John in prison".
John had told him, "It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife." Matthew says Herod would have put him to death but "feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet".
Mark says Herodias wanted John dead, "but she could not: For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy", and "heard him gladly".

At his birthday supper the daughter of Herodias danced; he swore to give her whatever she asked, "unto the half of my kingdom". Prompted by her mother she asked for "the head of John the Baptist". "The king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath's sake" he sent and had John beheaded in the prison.

Hearing of Jesus' works, he said, "It is John, whom I beheaded: he is risen from the dead." In Luke he is "perplexed": "John have I beheaded: but who is this, of whom I hear such things? And he desired to see him."
Some Pharisees warned Jesus, "Herod will kill thee." Jesus answered, "Go ye, and tell that fox, Behold, I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow".
Jesus warned his disciples to "beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and of the leaven of Herod".

At the trial Pilate sent Jesus to Herod, who "was exceeding glad" and "hoped to have seen some miracle done by him". He questioned him "in many words; but he answered him nothing". Herod and his soldiers "set him at nought, and mocked him, and arrayed him in a gorgeous robe", and sent him back.
"The same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together." Pilate told the accusers, "No, nor yet Herod" had found anything worthy of death in Jesus.
The church in Jerusalem said in prayer that "both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together" against Jesus.
Among those near him: Joanna, "the wife of Chuza Herod's steward", who ministered to Jesus; and Manaen of the church at Antioch, "brought up with Herod the tetrarch".

claim.text: He married Herodias, "his brother Philip's wife".
He shut up John in prison after John reproved him.
At his birthday supper he granted the head of John the Baptist.
He thought John had risen, and desired to see Jesus.
Warned that Herod would kill him, Jesus sent word to "that fox".
At Jerusalem he questioned and mocked Jesus and sent him back to Pilate.

worship.text: He was in Jerusalem at the Passover of Jesus' trial: "who himself also was at Jerusalem at that time".

alliances.text: Before the trial Pilate and he "were at enmity between themselves"; that day they became friends.

people.text: His birthday supper was for "his lords, high captains, and chief estates of Galilee".

claim.text: John reproved him over Herodias "and for all the evils which Herod had done", and was imprisoned and beheaded for it.

quote.text: It is not lawful for thee to have her.

claim.text: Pilate sent Jesus to him and he sent Jesus back; "the same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together".

rulers.name: Aretas
rulers.note: Aretas IV; Schürer (1890) takes the Aretas of 2 Corinthians 11:32 to be the same king

claim.text: Schürer (1890) dates Aretas IV from 9 BC to AD 40, puts his war with Antipas in AD 36, and identifies him with the King Aretas whose governor held Damascus when Paul escaped (2 Corinthians 11:32).

Schürer (1890) reports coins inscribed, in Greek, "of Herod the tetrarch", some bearing the name Tiberias, the latest of his forty-third year, which he dates to AD 39–40; like his father's, they carry no image.

twoAccounts.topic: Did Herod himself want John dead?

first.text: Matthew: "when he would have put him to death, he feared the multitude".

second.text: Mark: Herodias "would have killed him; but she could not: For Herod feared John".

questions.question: Where were John's prison and Herod's banquet?

views.label: In Galilee, perhaps Tiberias
views.holders: Keim and Volkmar, as reported by Schürer (1890)

argument.text: They read Mark's guests, the "chief estates of Galilee", as placing the supper in Galilee. Schürer answers that the Gospels do not name the place.
Wieseler moved the scene to Julias; Schürer sees no reason for it.

views.label: A looser, popular use of "king"
views.holders: H. A. W. Meyer (English 1880), after Theophylact

argument.text: Matthew and Luke call him tetrarch, Mark "king Herod" (and Matthew too says "the king was sorry"). Meyer calls Mark's title "a more popular but less accurate term".
Schürer says Matthew 14:1 and Luke 3:19 name him correctly and Mark 6:14 incorrectly calls him king.

notSaid: Scripture never uses the name Antipas; it calls him Herod.
The Gospels do not name the place where John was imprisoned and killed.
Scripture does not name the daughter of Herodias.
Scripture does not record how his rule ended.
Scripture does not say who the Herodians were (Matthew 22:16; Mark 3:6; 12:13), or how they were connected with him.
Scripture does not say why Pilate and Herod had been at enmity.

rulers.name: Philip the tetrarch
rulers.title: Tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis, under Rome
rulers.tagline: Named once, in Luke's dating of John's preaching.

identifications.text: Luke names "his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis", the brother of Herod the tetrarch of Galilee.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: None. Luke names him in the fifteenth year of Tiberius (Luke 3:1).

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: Tetrarch from 4 BC; died in the winter of AD 33/34, in the twentieth year of Tiberius.

scriptureSays.text: "In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar", when John began to preach, Philip, Herod's brother, was "tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis".
This is the only verse that names him. Scripture records no word or deed of his, and no meeting with Jesus.

claim.text: Luke names him among the rulers when John's preaching began.

worship.text: Schürer (1890) reports that Philip's coins carry the heads of Augustus and Tiberius and a temple, which he takes to be Herod's temple of Augustus at Paneas, the first likeness of an emperor on the coins of a Jewish prince; he explains it by a population mainly not Jewish.

people.text: Schürer (1890) describes the population of his tetrarchy as mixed, with the Syrian and Greek element prevailing.

claim.text: Luke dates his tetrarchy by "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar", with Pontius Pilate governor of Judaea.
Schürer (1890) notes that the Paneas district had once belonged to the Iturean kingdom, so Luke's statement is "not altogether incorrect", though Ituraea proper, in the Lebanon, was never Philip's.

Schürer (1890) identifies the Gospels' Caesarea Philippi with the city Philip rebuilt at Paneas, but thought Philip's Bethsaida-Julias was probably a different place from the Bethsaida of the Gospels.

questions.question: When was "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius" (Luke 3:1)?

argument.text: Schürer (1890) reckons Luke's fifteenth year as running from August AD 28 to August AD 29, and so dates John's first preaching then.
Counted from the year when Tiberius first shared authority over the provinces with Augustus; Ramsay finds Luke's statements of time then consistent.

notSaid: Only Luke 3:1 names him; Scripture records no word or deed of his.
Scripture does not say that Philip built Caesarea Philippi.
The "Philip" whose wife Herodias had been (Mark 6:17) is, on most views, a different man.
Scripture does not say whether its Bethsaida is the town Philip renamed Julias.

rulers.name: Herod Agrippa I
rulers.title: King over Judaea, under Rome
rulers.tagline: The king who killed James and imprisoned Peter.

identifications.text: Acts calls him only "Herod the king". He acts in Judaea, goes down "from Judaea to Caesarea", and dies there. Acts never calls him Agrippa and does not say whose son he was.
Eusebius (about AD 325) heads his chapter on Acts 12 "Agrippa, who was also called Herod" (Church History 2.10).
He is not the "Herod the tetrarch" of Acts 13:1, the verse after his story ends; that is Herod Antipas.

dates.label: Scripture's numbers
dates.note: None. Acts sets his persecution "about that time", after the famine foretold for "the days of Claudius Caesar" (Acts 11:28; 12:1).

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: King of Philip's former tetrarchy from AD 37, of Antipas's from about AD 40, of Judaea and Samaria from AD 41; died at Caesarea in AD 44.

scriptureSays.text: "Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church. And he killed James the brother of John with the sword."

"Because he saw it pleased the Jews, he proceeded further to take Peter also", in "the days of unleavened bread". He set four quaternions of soldiers to guard him, "intending after Easter to bring him forth to the people".
The KJV's "Easter" in Acts 12:4 translates the same Greek word it renders "Passover" in Luke 22:1.

The church prayed without ceasing. On the night before Herod would have brought him out, an angel freed Peter, who said, "the Lord hath sent his angel, and hath delivered me out of the hand of Herod".
"When Herod had sought for him, and found him not, he examined the keepers, and commanded that they should be put to death." Then he went down from Judaea to Caesarea.
He "was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon"; through Blastus, "the king's chamberlain", they asked for peace, "because their country was nourished by the king's country".

"Upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration". The people shouted, "It is the voice of a god, and not of a man." "And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost."
"But the word of God grew and multiplied."

claim.text: He killed James the brother of John with the sword.
He imprisoned Peter at the Passover season; an angel freed him; the keepers were put to death.
Tyre and Sidon sought peace with him through Blastus.
Hailed as a god after his oration, he was smitten by the angel of the Lord and died.

worship.text: He seized Peter because "he saw it pleased the Jews".

alliances.text: Tyre and Sidon depended on "the king's country" for food and sought peace with him.

people.text: At Caesarea "the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man."

claim.text: Acts sets his persecution "about that time", after Agabus foretold a dearth "which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar".

rulers.name: Blastus
rulers.note: the king's chamberlain, through whom they sought peace

claim.text: The two cities sought peace "because their country was nourished by the king's country".

questions.question: When in AD 44 did he die?

views.label: 6 August 44, at the regular games founded by Herod
views.holders: Wieseler, followed by A. C. McGiffert (1890)

argument.text: McGiffert thinks the festival was more probably the five-yearly games Herod the Great instituted for Augustus, and gives Wieseler's date of 6 August 44.

notSaid: Acts never calls him Agrippa, and does not say whose son or grandson he was.
Acts does not say why he was displeased with Tyre and Sidon.
Acts gives no year for his death.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where he killed James and imprisoned Peter (Acts 12 does not name the city)

rulers.name: Agrippa II
otherNames: Marcus Julius Agrippa (coins and inscriptions, by Schürer)
rulers.title: King under Rome, of lands north and east of Galilee
rulers.tagline: The king who heard Paul's defence at Caesarea.

identifications.text: Acts calls him "king Agrippa" and sets him beside Bernice in the time of the governor Festus. Acts never calls him Herod and does not say who his father was.
Schürer (1890) places the visit of Acts 25:13 in AD 60, when Agrippa and Bernice came "with great pomp" to welcome the new procurator Festus.

dates.label: Schürer (1890)
dates.note: King of Chalcis from about AD 50; of Philip's former tetrarchy from AD 53, with parts of Galilee and Perea added by Nero; died in the third year of Trajan, AD 100, by the report of Justus of Tiberias preserved by Photius.

scriptureSays.text: "King Agrippa and Bernice came unto Caesarea to salute Festus." Festus laid Paul's case before him: a man "left in bonds by Felix", accused over questions "of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive".
Agrippa said, "I would also hear the man myself."

Next day Agrippa and Bernice came "with great pomp" into the place of hearing. Festus said he had "no certain thing to write unto my lord" and had brought Paul "specially before thee, O king Agrippa".

"Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Thou art permitted to speak for thyself." Paul called himself happy to answer before him, "because I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews".

Paul told of his life as a Pharisee, his persecuting, the light and voice on the road to Damascus, and his preaching; he said, "the king knoweth of these things ... for this thing was not done in a corner."
"King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest. Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian."

Rising with the governor and Bernice, they agreed, "This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds", and Agrippa said to Festus, "This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar."

claim.text: With Bernice he greeted Festus and heard Paul's defence.

alliances.text: He came to Caesarea to greet the new governor Festus, who consulted him about Paul.
Schürer (1890): through the war of 66–70 he stood on the Roman side; he hosted Vespasian at Caesarea Philippi and was with Titus.

people.text: Bernice sat with him at Paul's hearing and rose with him and the governor.

Suetonius writes of Titus's "notorious passion for queen Berenice, to whom it was even said that he promised marriage", and that as emperor he sent her from Rome "against her will and against his own" (Titus 7).

claim.text: Festus had come "into Felix' room" and inherited Paul as a prisoner; he laid the case before Agrippa.
Schürer (1890) reports coins of Agrippa bearing the names of Nero, Vespasian, Titus and Domitian; one of his thirty-fifth year shows him alive in AD 95 at least.
Suetonius, Titus 7: Titus's passion for "queen Berenice", and her dismissal from Rome when he became emperor.

questions.question: What did Agrippa mean by "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian" (Acts 26:28)?

views.label: Almost persuaded, and in earnest
views.holders: the KJV's rendering, following Chrysostom; J. A. Bengel (1742); John Gill (1746–1748); Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871)

argument.text: They read the words as a real admission that Paul had nearly won him; Bengel sees "a motion towards good in him", and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown argue that Paul's reply ("both almost, and altogether") suits only that sense.

views.label: "With little persuasion": a dismissive answer
views.holders: H. A. W. Meyer (English 1877–1879); C. J. Ellicott's commentary (about 1880); J. R. Lumby (1882)

argument.text: They hold that the Greek means "with little" (effort, words or time), not "almost", and read the reply as mockery: Ellicott calls it "a cynical sneer", and Lumby cites the Revised Version's "With but little persuasion thou wouldest fain make me a Christian".

notSaid: Acts never calls him Herod, and does not say whose son he was.
Acts does not say how Bernice was related to him.
Acts records his words to Paul but says nothing of his faith beyond them.
